clue.text: John, giving evidence, will spring a surprise

parts.note: Jack is the familiar pet form of the name John
a witness giving evidence stands in the witness box

explanation.surface: A man called John takes the stand in court and is about to drop a bombshell.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description of the toy rather than a synonym: it is the boxed figure that leaps out when the lid opens.
explanation.definitionFit: This toy is a lidded case from which a sprung figure leaps out to startle a child.

clue.text: Judge asking for no lemon in his gin and tonic?

parts.note: a drinker refusing the lemon slice asks for 'just' the other thing
the frozen cubes that go in a gin and tonic

explanation.surface: A judge orders a gin and tonic and specifies no lemon.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a bar order; the judge sense of the answer is the title of English High Court judges.
explanation.definitionFit: Justice is a title for a judge, as in Mr Justice Smith in the English courts.

clue.text: Daily, Edward marked his position

parts.note: a daily is a British term for a cleaning woman, also called a char
Ted is a short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: Edward, a newspaper man, notes where he stands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' looks like a newspaper, but in British usage a daily is a cleaner who comes in each day, a char.
explanation.definitionFit: A navigator who plots a ship's place on a map has charted it.

clue.text: Try and incite revolution, going from one town to another

definitions.text: going from one town to another

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Agitators try to stir up rebellion as they travel from town to town.
explanation.definitionFit: Intercity describes travel or trains running between major towns.

clue.text: Get drier coming from Bath to Wells

indicators.note: the answer comes out of the run of letters across these place names

explanation.surface: Someone drying off on a journey between two Somerset cities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming from' shows the answer sits inside 'Bath to Wells'; Bath and Wells are cities in Somerset, England, and a bath suggests drying.
explanation.definitionFit: To rub yourself down with a cloth after washing is to make yourself dry.

clue.text: Enter to change a pound? Can't be changed

indicators.note: the letters are to be changed into a new order

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Someone asks a cashier for change for a pound coin and is refused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to change' rearranges ENTER and A into ETERNA; L follows. The later 'changed' is the definition, a neat contrast.
explanation.definitionFit: Something everlasting never alters.

clue.text: Old Turk's sofa

explanation.surface: An elderly Turkish man's couch.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ottoman Empire was the old Turkish state, and an upholstered seat without a back or arms also bears the name.

clue.text: Tip shampoo up-what a mess, you beast!

indicators.note: a mess of letters signals that the preceding words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone tips a bottle of shampoo over and scolds the animal responsible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what a mess' rearranges the twelve letters of TIP SHAMPOO UP.
explanation.definitionFit: The hippo is a large African animal, so it is a beast.

clue.text: Pressing for a moment

explanation.surface: Something urgent, needing attention right away.
explanation.definitionFit: Urgent business is instant in an old sense, and a moment is a brief point in time.

clue.text: Grabbed wicket and relaxed

parts.note: W is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a wicket
relaxed means rested, taken a break

explanation.surface: A cricketer seizes a wicket and then takes it easy.
explanation.walkthrough: W for wicket is a cricket scoring convention.
explanation.definitionFit: To seize something by force or twisting is to have wrenched it away.

clue.text: No food still at these formal balls?

definitions.text: No food still at these formal balls?

parts.words: No food still at these formal balls?
parts.note: read as evening meal plus moves on a floor: at such balls the meal comes first, yet the joke is that guests dance instead of eating

explanation.surface: A complaint that a smart ball has served nothing to eat yet.
explanation.walkthrough: A whimsical cryptic definition of social events combining an evening meal with ballroom dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: These are formal evening functions where a meal is followed by ballroom dancing.

clue.text: Watercolourist's line

explanation.surface: An artist's characteristic brushstroke.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist working in watercolours makes pictures, and a mooring rope on a boat's bow is also so called.

clue.text: Continuity announcer had connection with island

parts.note: a link is a connection
Man is the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: A broadcaster linked to an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man is an island between Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A presenter who ties together items in a broadcast is the one who keeps the programme flowing.

clue.text: Dupes led astray by hypocrite

indicators.note: letters led off the right path end up in a different order

explanation.surface: Gullible people are misled by a two-faced fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: A poseur pretending to culture or learning is a kind of fraud.

clue.text: One thousand scales show bias

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
a pair of scales is a balance for weighing

explanation.surface: A thousand weighings reveal a lean one way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scales' is a noun here, the weighing instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A lack of evenness between sides is a lean or prejudice.

clue.text: Hear animal sing curiously, producing its first milk

indicators.note: heard spoken, the word for an animal gives the opening sound

parts.note: a beast is an animal

indicators.note: curiously signals the letters of sing appear in an odd order

explanation.surface: A listener hears a creature sing strangely while a newborn is fed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear' gives BEEST from BEAST; 'curiously' rearranges SING into INGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Beestings is the colostrum a cow gives after calving, the earliest milk.

clue.text: Apply for loan to character, but don't look as you tap

parts.note: to touch someone for money is to ask them for a loan
type is a printed character

explanation.surface: Advice to a typist: write a begging letter but keep your eyes off the keys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touch' for asking someone for money is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Typing by feel on a keyboard means working without watching your fingers.

clue.text: Manic condition of northern New York, say?

explanation.surface: Asking whether a frenzy is typical of the northern part of a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: A manic mood is a high, elated frame of mind, and the rural north of New York State is the region away from the city.

clue.text: Despicable person to solicit dregs from glass

parts.note: a heel is a contemptible man
to tap someone is to ask them for money

explanation.surface: A cad cadges the last drops from a drinking glass.
explanation.definitionFit: The small residue left in a drinking vessel is the bit at the bottom.

clue.text: Drench with light

explanation.surface: Soaking something and bathing it in illumination.
explanation.definitionFit: To deluge is to soak completely, and a powerful lamp for a stage or stadium bears the same name.

clue.text: Russian jeweller altered bag, free

indicators.note: the letters of the words are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A jeweller in Russia has changed a bag and it costs nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Carl Faberge was the goldsmith to the Russian tsars, famous for jewelled eggs.

clue.text: Unfashionable rules for old villains

parts.note: out means no longer in fashion
laws are rules

explanation.surface: Dated regulations governing villains of yesteryear.
explanation.definitionFit: Bandits declared beyond legal protection were the criminals of earlier times.

clue.text: Is lamed awkwardly, and has bad hand

indicators.note: letters arranged awkwardly fall into a clumsy new order

explanation.surface: A card player injured and holding poor cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrong distribution of cards gives a player a faulty set.

clue.text: Sort of corporal's weapon?

explanation.surface: Asking about a junior soldier's arms.
explanation.definitionFit: A lance corporal is the lowest NCO rank in the British Army, and a long spear carried by a knight is a weapon.

clue.text: Container holds letter from abroad-one from Lhasa

indicators.note: one word holds another within it

parts.note: a tin is a container
beta is a foreign letter, from the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A box arrives containing a letter posted from a far-off city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter from abroad' looks like a posted letter; it is a Greek alphabet character.
explanation.definitionFit: Lhasa is the capital of Tibet, so a native of it belongs to that people.

clue.text: Piece of wood to beat ascetic

parts.note: a spar is a pole or beam of wood
to tan someone is to thrash them

explanation.surface: Using a stick to thrash a hermit.
explanation.definitionFit: The citizens of ancient Sparta were famed for self-denial, so the word means austere.

clue.text: Hurried back to assess recount

indicators.note: back says the word for hurried is turned around

parts.note: hurried means ran
to rate is to assess

explanation.surface: Someone rushes back to put a value on a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns RAN into NAR. 'recount' looks like counting again; it means tell.
explanation.definitionFit: To tell a story is to relate it.

clue.text: Weak head found in a state without assistance

parts.note: helpless means weak, powerless
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbour names like Sheerness

explanation.surface: A frail leader is found in a country with no aid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' is a headland, NESS, common in British place names.
explanation.definitionFit: The condition of being unable to cope on one's own is a dependent state.
